title: The key purpose of project management
blurb: State why project management exists: to deliver beneficial change within agreed constraints.
question: Lakeside Council's board is asked to pay for a project manager on its new flood defence scheme. A councillor asks: 'What is project management actually FOR?' What is the best one-sentence answer?

teach.h: One purpose: beneficial change, delivered successfully
teach.body: The key purpose of project management is to deliver the planned objectives for change successfully: in short, to bring about beneficial change. In practice that means delivering the agreed outputs, and enabling the outcomes and benefits they lead to, within the agreed constraints of time, cost, quality and scope. Every plan, register and meeting a project manager uses exists to serve that one purpose.

Change is risky. Lakeside Council must build a flood wall before winter, within its budget, to a standard that actually holds back the river. Left to chance, work like this overruns, overspends or delivers something that doesn't do the job. Project management gives the change structure (clear objectives, plans and roles), control (drift is spotted and corrected) and visibility (the sponsor sees real progress and risks).

teach.h: Lakeside's flood scheme: the purpose in action

steps.label: Project management
steps.sub: Plans, organises and controls the work

steps.label: Outputs
steps.sub: Flood wall and pumps, on time and budget

steps.label: Beneficial change
steps.sub: Homes stay dry; insurance becomes affordable

teach.caption: Project management is the engine between the need and the beneficial change.

items.label: the agreed schedule: built before winter
the agreed budget for the scheme
fit for purpose: it must hold back the river
the agreed outputs: wall, pumps, gates

teach.caption: Delivering the outputs is not enough on its own. Success means delivering them within these agreed limits.

teach.h: How project management achieves its purpose

root.label: Deliver beneficial change
root.sub: within time, cost, quality and scope

head: Project management gives…
So that…
rows: Everyone knows the objectives, plan and their role
Drift is spotted early and changes are approved, not slipped in
The sponsor sees true progress and risk, and can decide in time
Effort goes into what delivers the change, not side tasks

teach.body: Time, cost, quality and scope are linked: change one and the others feel it. Halfway through, residents ask Lakeside to add a riverside cycle path. More scope means more cost, a later finish, or both. Part of the purpose of project management is to make those trade-offs visible so the sponsor can decide deliberately, rather than letting them happen by accident.

teach.text: Distractors dress up a tool or a nice side effect as THE purpose: 'to produce plans and reports', 'to please every stakeholder', 'to eliminate risk', 'to control the team'. Plans and reports are tools; happy stakeholders are a welcome result; risk can be managed but never removed. The purpose is beneficial change, delivered within agreed constraints.

rows.label: Flood wall built before winter, within budget
Every resident loves the wall's design
Zero risk of anything going wrong

teach.h: Tools serve the purpose, not the other way round
teach.caption: Read it bottom to top: the means at the base exist only to deliver what sits at the top.

items: Key purpose: deliver the planned objectives for change successfully, i.e. bring about beneficial change.
That means delivering the agreed outputs (and enabling outcomes and benefits) within time, cost, quality and scope.
It does this by planning, organising, controlling, managing risk and directing people.
It gives change structure, control and visibility. It cannot remove all risk or please everyone.

summary: You can now state the key purpose of project management: to deliver the planned objectives for change successfully, bringing about beneficial change within agreed constraints of time, cost, quality and scope. You can also separate that purpose from the tools it uses and from tempting but wrong aims like removing all risk.

A.q: Which of the following best states the key purpose of project management?
options: To keep every stakeholder fully satisfied
To deliver the objectives for change successfully
To produce detailed plans and progress reports
To remove all uncertainty from the organisation's work
A.why: Project management exists to deliver the planned objectives for change successfully: to bring about beneficial change.

whyNot.0: Satisfied stakeholders are a welcome result, but pleasing everyone is neither possible nor the purpose.
whyNot.2: Plans and reports are tools project management uses, not its purpose.
whyNot.3: Uncertainty can be managed but never removed, especially in unique work.

A.q: Project management aims to deliver objectives within agreed constraints. Which set of constraints does this usually refer to?
options: Time, cost, quality and scope
Staff, offices, IT and suppliers
Policy, law, economy and society
Sales, profit, shares and growth
A.why: The agreed constraints are time, cost, quality and scope: deliver the right thing, to standard, on time and on budget.

whyNot.1: These are resources an organisation has, not the constraints a project is measured against.
whyNot.2: These resemble PESTLE factors in the external environment, not project constraints.
whyNot.3: These are business performance measures, not the project's agreed constraints.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the key purpose of project management?
options: Delivering the agreed outputs
Working within agreed constraints
Enabling beneficial change
Eliminating every project risk
A.why: Risk can be identified and managed, but never eliminated entirely; that is not the purpose of project management.

whyNot.0: Delivering the agreed outputs is central to the purpose.
whyNot.1: Delivering within time, cost, quality and scope is part of the purpose.
whyNot.2: Beneficial change is the whole reason project management exists.

B.q: A sponsor cannot tell whether her project is on track until it finishes. Which benefit of project management is she missing?
options: A larger budget held for contingency
Visibility of true progress and risk
A guarantee that all stakeholders approve
Freedom from any change requests
B.why: Project management gives visibility: regular, honest information on progress and risk so the sponsor can decide in time.

whyNot.0: Contingency is useful, but it would not tell her whether the project is on track.
whyNot.2: No approach can guarantee every stakeholder approves.
whyNot.3: Change requests still happen; project management controls them rather than preventing them.

B.q:
Which THREE of the following help project management achieve its purpose?
1) Planning the work
2) Managing risk
3) Controlling progress
4) Avoiding all change
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
B.why: Planning (1), managing risk (2) and controlling progress (3) are how project management delivers objectives within constraints.

whyNot.1: Item 4 is wrong: projects exist to make change, and requested changes are controlled, not avoided.
whyNot.2: Item 4 is wrong, and managing risk (2) is missing.
whyNot.3: Item 4 is wrong, and planning the work (1) is missing.

B.q: Halfway through a flood wall project, residents ask for a cycle path to be added. What does the purpose of project management call for?
options: Accept it quietly to keep the residents happy
Refuse it, because scope can never be changed
Add it and simply keep the original end date
Assess its impact on time, cost and quality
B.why: Extra scope affects the other constraints. Assessing the impact lets the sponsor make an informed decision on the trade-off.

whyNot.0: Accepting changes without assessing them causes overruns and loss of control.
whyNot.1: Scope can change, but only through a controlled decision; refusing outright is not the purpose.
whyNot.2: Adding scope while ignoring its effect on time and cost is how projects overrun.

C.q: A project delivered its outputs on time and on budget, but nobody uses them, so nothing changes. Judged against the key purpose of project management, how did it do?
options: It succeeded, as its time and cost targets were met
It succeeded, because its outputs were delivered
It fell short, as no beneficial change resulted
It fell short, because it had a set budget to use
C.why: The purpose is beneficial change. Outputs that are never used deliver no change, so the purpose was not achieved.

whyNot.0: Meeting time and cost is necessary but not sufficient; the change has to happen.
whyNot.1: Outputs are the means; unused outputs bring no benefit.
whyNot.3: Every project has a budget; having one is not why it fell short.

C.q: Which statement best describes how project management adds value to an organisation?
options: It brings structure, control and visibility to change
It replaces business as usual with temporary teams
It ensures that every project is approved and funded
It lets work begin without any agreed objectives at all
C.why: Project management gives change structure (objectives, plans, roles), control (correcting drift) and visibility (true progress and risk).

whyNot.1: Projects hand outputs into BAU; they do not replace it.
whyNot.2: Some projects should rightly be rejected or stopped; approval is a governance decision.
whyNot.3: Agreed objectives are the starting point of project management, not something it removes.

C.q: A sponsor asks why she should fund a project manager for a six-month IT upgrade. Which reply best reflects the key purpose of project management?
options: So the IT team gains a permanent manager once it goes live
So the upgrade's objectives are met within agreed limits
So the upgrade needs no further input from the sponsor
So every user receives every feature that they ask for
C.why: A project manager is there to deliver the upgrade's objectives for change within the agreed time, cost, quality and scope.

whyNot.0: Project roles are temporary; running the system afterwards is BAU.
whyNot.2: The sponsor stays accountable throughout and must make key decisions.
whyNot.3: Scope is agreed and controlled; giving everyone everything would break the constraints.

reteach.title: Building a house extension
reteach.question: A couple are extending their house before their baby arrives in June. Is the point of managing the build to produce drawings and spreadsheets, or something else?

blocks.h: The point is the change, within limits
blocks.body: Drawings, a schedule and a budget spreadsheet are useful, but they are not why the couple are managing the build. The point is a finished extension that gives them a bigger family kitchen (the beneficial change), delivered within the limits they agreed: ready before June, within £60,000, built to regulations and including exactly what they asked for.

head: Constraint
For the extension
rows: Finished before the baby arrives in June
Within the £60,000 agreed with the bank
Warm, dry, signed off by building control

blocks.text: A beautiful extension finished in October, £20,000 over budget, has not achieved the purpose: the constraints were part of the deal. Equally, a perfect plan for an extension never built achieves nothing.

explain.body: Organisations don't fund project management for its own sake. They fund it because they need change to happen successfully: a new service, system, building or way of working that leaves them better off.

test.q: Why does an organisation invest in project management at all?
options: To create more management job roles
To keep its operations exactly as is
To make change happen successfully
To reduce the need for any planning
test.why: Project management exists to make change happen successfully: to deliver the planned objectives for change.

whyNot.0: Creating job roles is not a purpose; project roles are temporary.
whyNot.1: Keeping operations unchanged is the aim of BAU, the opposite of a project.
whyNot.3: Project management increases good planning; it does not remove the need for it.

explain.body: Success is not 'delivered, eventually, at any cost'. It is delivering the agreed scope, to the agreed quality, on time and within budget. These four constraints are agreed up front and are what the project is measured against.

test.q: Which of the following is one of the agreed constraints that project management works within?
options: Headcount
Quality
Morale
Turnover
test.why: Quality, along with time, cost and scope, is one of the agreed constraints a project is delivered within.

whyNot.0: Headcount is a resource measure, not one of the four constraints.
whyNot.2: Team morale matters, but it is not a project constraint.
whyNot.3: Turnover (sales or staff) is a business measure, not a project constraint.

explain.body: Project management achieves its purpose by planning the work, organising people and resources, controlling progress against the plan, managing risk and directing the team. Control is the activity that keeps the project inside its constraints.

test.q: Which activity is most directly about keeping a project within its agreed constraints?
options: Writing the organisation's strategy
Running routine operational tasks
Recruiting permanent department staff
Monitoring and controlling progress
test.why: Monitoring progress against the plan and taking corrective action keeps time, cost, quality and scope on track.

whyNot.0: Strategy is set at organisational level; projects support it but don't write it.
whyNot.1: Routine operational tasks are business as usual.
whyNot.2: Recruiting permanent staff is an HR (BAU) activity.

explain.body: Schedules, plans, registers and reports are tools that serve the purpose. If an exam option names a document or a technique, ask: is that the end goal, or a means to it? The end goal is always beneficial change within constraints.

test.q: Which of the following is a tool of project management rather than its purpose?
options: Achieving the planned objectives
Delivering beneficial change
Producing a project schedule
Meeting the agreed constraints
test.why: A schedule is a tool that helps deliver the objectives; it is not the purpose itself.

whyNot.0: Achieving the planned objectives is the purpose.
whyNot.1: Delivering beneficial change is the purpose.
whyNot.3: Meeting the agreed constraints is part of delivering the purpose successfully.
